safety.description: Blend of crime rate, pedestrian/cyclist crash rate, FEMA natural hazard risk, and chronic disease burden (all inverted: lower = higher safety)

opportunity.description: Blended 85/15 with a Census ACS educational-attainment score (share of adults with a bachelor's+; district-level only, like broadband). Base blend of permit rate (more development = higher opportunity), unemployment rate (more unemployment = lower opportunity), and Zillow for-sale housing inventory per capita. NOTE: housing_market's direction is a deliberate but debatable modeling choice — fewer listings is treated as a 'tighter, more in-demand market' (higher Opportunity), the seller's-market reading. An equally defensible buyer's-market reading would treat fewer listings as LESS opportunity (harder to find a home to buy into). Revisit if this doesn't match the intended meaning of Opportunity.

amenities.formula: 0.85 * normalize(schools_pc + grocery_pc + restaurants_pc + healthcare_pc + entertainment_pc) + 0.15 * normalize(broadband_rate)
amenities.description: Amenities & Services: a blended OpenStreetMap amenity-access sub-score (schools/groceries/restaurants/healthcare/entertainment, each 0.20), blended 85/15 with a Census ACS broadband/internet-access rate (share of households with an internet subscription; core/health_score.py's compute_broadband_index_combined). Trails, transit, and traffic moved to the Transportation component; chronic disease burden moved to Safety. Housing production and Service Requests were both removed: Housing production (see clean_housing_mpls.py/clean_housing.py docstrings) had no dedicated Minneapolis dataset — it was proxied from all residential permits (CCS_Permits, permitType='Res'), most of which are remodels/repairs with zero new dwelling units, undercounting Minneapolis (361 units) by ~5x versus St. Paul's dedicated new-construction dataset (1,834 units). Service Requests (request_rate_pc, see clean_requests_mpls.py) had a similar problem one level deeper: St. Paul's Resident Service Requests dataset is scoped narrowly to livability/code-enforcement complaints, while Minneapolis's 311 feed is a much broader all-purpose contact-center system covering categories St. Paul doesn't track (licensing/permitting, utility billing, animal complaints, police-adjacent reports) and logs the same complaint under separate categories per intake channel (call center vs. Open311 app/API). After excluding non-comparable categories and deduping likely same-incident channel duplicates, Minneapolis's per-capita rate was still ~3x St. Paul's with more taxonomy mismatches likely remaining — the two cities' complaint-tracking systems are too structurally different to make comparable without exhaustive, ongoing reconciliation.

transportation.description: Trail/path length and transit stop rate (direct) minus traffic volume (inverted), blended 60/25/15 with a Zillow-style Walk/Bike Score and a Census ACS commute score (average of inverted mean commute time and transit/walk/bike commute share; district-level only, like Walk/Bike Score). Walk/Bike Score (core/walk_score.py: distance-decay proximity to groceries/restaurants/transit/schools/healthcare + street-intersection density + trail km, computed separately from the per-source pipeline)

affordability.formula: average(100 - normalize(median_home_value), 100 - normalize(median_gross_rent), normalize(median_household_income), 100 - normalize(poverty_rate), 100 - normalize(housing_cost_burden_rate), normalize(homeownership_rate), 100 - normalize(gini_index), 100 - normalize(vacancy_rate))
affordability.description: Census ACS housing cost burden (2026-09-21: vacancy rate now included, lower = better, treated as a blight/disinvestment signal despite the ambiguity noted below): lower home values/rent/poverty/cost-burden/income-inequality (Gini index) and higher household income/homeownership relative to other districts raise this index. Gini added 2026-09-15 (see core/health_score.py's _affordability_index_from_df) — vacancy rate was also added to the pipeline around the same time but deliberately left out of the score since, unlike the other fields here, its 'good' direction is ambiguous (high vacancy can mean disinvestment or just a loose rental market); it's exposed in the sidebar as context only.

normalization.description: Each metric (e.g. crime_rate_pc, crash_rate_pc) is z-scored and squashed through a logistic curve to (0, 100) INDEPENDENTLY — not min-max scaled, and not pooled with other metrics in the same component before normalizing — then the normalized values are weight-averaged per the formulas above. Normalization is pooled across ALL districts in BOTH St. Paul and Minneapolis (28 districts), not per-city, so scores are directly comparable across cities. See core/health_score.py's min_max_normalize() (name kept for historical reasons; it is not min-max scaling) and compute_component_index().
